title: Does a Dehumidifier Help With Mold? Prevention vs. Removal
h1: Does a Dehumidifier Help With Mold?
dek: A dehumidifier is one of the best mold-prevention tools you can own. It just can't clean up the mold you already have — here's what can.
description: Dehumidifiers for mold prevention work by keeping humidity under 50–60%, but they don't kill existing mold. How to use one, clean up and when to call a pro.
intro: Yes — a dehumidifier helps with mold, but mostly in one direction. **Dehumidifiers for mold prevention** are genuinely effective: mold needs moisture to grow, and keeping indoor humidity below about 50–60% takes away the damp conditions it depends on. What a dehumidifier can't do is kill mold that's already growing or remove the stains, spores and musty smell it leaves behind.

That's an important distinction, because many people buy a dehumidifier hoping it will get rid of mold on a basement wall or bathroom ceiling. It won't. It will, however, stop that mold from spreading, help the area dry after cleanup and keep new growth from starting.
Below, we explain what the EPA recommends, how to set up a dehumidifier for mold control, how to clean up existing growth safely, and when the job is big enough to call a professional.

blocks.text: Those three numbers frame everything a dehumidifier can and can't do. It's excellent at the first, helpful with the second, and no substitute for proper cleanup once you've passed the third.

sections.heading: How a dehumidifier helps prevent mold

blocks.text: Mold spores are everywhere, indoors and out. They only become a problem when they land on something damp enough to grow on. By keeping the air at 30–50% humidity, a dehumidifier helps keep walls, carpets, stored boxes and wood dry enough that spores stay dormant.

items: **Basements:** stops the musty smell and mildew on stored items and drywall.
**Bathrooms and laundry rooms:** dries the room after showers and washing.
**Closets:** protects clothing and shoes from mildew.
**After cleanup:** dries the area so mold doesn't return.

sections.heading: Can a dehumidifier kill mold or get rid of mold spores?

blocks.text: No. Drying out mold makes it dormant, not dead, and dried mold can still release spores and allergens. A dehumidifier's filter is a basic dust screen, so it also won't meaningfully clear mold spores from the air. For airborne spores and mold allergies, pair it with an air purifier using a true HEPA filter — see our [dehumidifier vs. air purifier](/guides/dehumidifier-vs-air-purifier/) guide and [best dehumidifier for allergies](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-allergies/).

blocks.title: The order matters
blocks.text: Fix the water source, clean up the mold, then use the dehumidifier to keep the space dry. Skipping straight to the dehumidifier leaves the existing mold in place.

sections.heading: How to get rid of mold: cleanup steps

blocks.text: For small areas, under roughly 10 square feet, the EPA says most homeowners can handle cleanup themselves:

items: **Stop the moisture.** Repair leaks, redirect downspouts and fix condensation problems first, or the mold will return.
**Protect yourself.** Wear an N95 respirator, gloves and goggles without vents.
**Scrub hard surfaces.** Use detergent and water on tile, glass, metal and sealed wood, then dry them completely.
**Remove porous materials.** Moldy ceiling tiles, carpet padding and drywall often need to be cut out and replaced.
**Don't paint over it.** Paint or caulk applied over mold tends to peel and lets growth continue underneath.
**Dry everything.** Run a dehumidifier and fans until surfaces are fully dry, then keep humidity below 50%.

blocks.text: If you use a cleaning product, follow its label exactly and never mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners, which can create toxic fumes.

sections.heading: When to call a mold remediation professional

items: The moldy area is larger than about 10 square feet.
Mold is inside walls, the HVAC system or ductwork.
The water damage came from sewage or flooding.
Someone in the home has asthma, allergies or a weakened immune system.
Mold keeps coming back after cleanup.

blocks.text: Professionals use containment, HEPA vacuums and commercial LGR dehumidifiers to dry structures quickly. Ask whether they'll find and fix the moisture source, not just remove the visible growth.

sections.heading: What to look for in a dehumidifier for mold control

items.label: Enough capacity
items.text: A damp basement generally needs 50 pints; a bathroom or bedroom 20–35. See our [dehumidifier size guide](/guides/dehumidifier-size-guide/).

items.label: Continuous drainage
items.text: A pump or hose keeps humidity from rebounding when a bucket fills.

items.label: A set-point humidistat
items.text: Set it to 45–50% and let it cycle.

items.label: Low-temperature operation
items.text: Cool basements need auto-defrost to keep working.

items.label: Easy cleaning
items.text: A dirty bucket can grow mold itself. Our [dehumidifier maintenance guide](/guides/dehumidifier-maintenance/) covers what to clean and when.

blocks.text: A dehumidifier is one of the best tools for mold prevention, but it won't kill mold or remove what's already there. Fix the moisture source, clean up small areas yourself or call a pro for anything over about 10 square feet, then run a dehumidifier to hold humidity at 30–50%. For a basement, the **Frigidaire FFAP5033W1** does that job well; after a leak, rent an LGR unit like the **Dri-Eaz Revolution**; and track it all with a hygrometer such as the **Govee H5075**.

faqs.q: Will a dehumidifier get rid of mold?
faqs.a: No. It stops mold from spreading and prevents new growth by keeping humidity low, but it doesn't kill or remove existing mold. Clean small areas with detergent and water, remove damaged porous materials, and call a professional for large areas.
The EPA recommends keeping indoor relative humidity below 60%, ideally between 30% and 50%. Most homeowners set their dehumidifier to 45–50%.

faqs.q: Do dehumidifiers help with mold allergies?
faqs.a: They help indirectly by preventing new mold growth, which reduces future spore levels. For spores already in the air, an air purifier with a true HEPA filter does more.

faqs.q: Can a dehumidifier remove mold spores from the air?
faqs.a: Not meaningfully. Its filter catches dust, not microscopic spores. A HEPA air purifier is the right tool for airborne spores; the dehumidifier keeps them from finding moisture to grow on.

faqs.q: What kind of dehumidifier is used for mold remediation?
faqs.a: Professionals typically use low-grain refrigerant (LGR) commercial dehumidifiers, which keep pulling moisture as the air gets drier. Homeowners can often rent one after a leak or flood.

faqs.q: Should I run a dehumidifier after mold cleanup?
faqs.a: Yes. Run it with fans until everything is fully dry, then keep it running on a humidistat at 45–50% to prevent mold from coming back.
